Stories / Madrid · Netherlands · 1578

Story · Monarchy of Philip II, 16th century

Madrid, 1578: “not a real”, Antonio Pérez writes in cipher to Don John of Austria

Summer 1578. Don John of Austria, half-brother of Philip II and victor of Lepanto, governs the Netherlands in revolt and asks for money for his army. In Madrid the Secretary of State Antonio Pérez answers him in his own hand on 19 August. Four months earlier Pérez had had Don John’s secretary, Juan de Escobedo, murdered in a Madrid street. In his letter, cordial in clear, the words that matter are in cipher.

Story by Brice Dudout · reading with Claude · document: Real Academia de la Historia (Madrid), 2/Ms Caja 8 nº 4 · published 14 November 2026

« … con grandissima dificultad del consejo de hazienda, por no aver un real y tantas cosas que proveer. »

“… with very great difficulty on the part of the Council of Finance, for there is not a real and so many things to provide for”: Antonio Pérez to Don John of Austria, Madrid, 19 August 1578 (ciphered passage).

What is new, what was known

Known. The Pérez–Escobedo affair is one of the most studied of Philip II’s reign, since Mignet (1845) and the documents published by Gaspar Muro (1877).[3][4] Don John’s lack of money is known, as is the Crown’s struggle, after the suspension of payments of 1575, to finance the war in Flanders. The letter, kept in the Fernández San Román collection of the Real Academia de la Historia, is online under the Public Domain Mark.[1]

What we add, to our knowledge. (1) The first published decipherment of the four ciphered passages: 70 words, 69 certain or probable (98.6%), read under Daniel Bourdeau’s rule. (2) The identification of the cipher: the numerical syllabary of the Spanish chancery of 1577, that of the Genoa despatches, with variants of Pérez’s own. (3) What Pérez hid from the clear text: the money does not exist.

Don John, Escobedo, Pérez

Don John was appointed governor of the Netherlands in 1576. After the Perpetual Edict of 1577 the war resumed; in January 1578 he beat the States General at Gembloux, but his ill-paid army was wearing down.[5] His secretary Escobedo had come to Madrid to defend his plans; Pérez presented him to the king as dangerous. On 31 March 1578 Escobedo was killed with swords in an alley; suspicion fell on Pérez, who still enjoyed the king’s trust.[4]

In August Don John sent Don Alonso de Sotomayor to Madrid to ask for funds. Pérez’s answer announces an asiento, a loan contract with bankers, and barely hides the essential.

What the cipher says

The first passage says the courier’s despatch was made “with very great difficulty” on the part of the Council of Finance, “for there is not a real and so many things to provide for”. The second adds:

“… the finances being so straitened that I hold it impossible to be able to supply as much as is needed.”

The third makes clear that the Council of Finance accepted the asiento only “under protest that no other will be honoured”. In other words: this money is the last. The clear text on the same page reports the defeat and death of King Sebastian of Portugal at Alcácer-Quibir on 4 August: a succession crisis was opening in Lisbon, which would absorb Philip II’s attention and money.

Don John died six weeks later, on 1 October 1578, near Namur, ill and without reinforcements. Pérez was arrested in July 1579. The letter of 19 August shows the Secretary of State at a precise moment: he keeps up a friendly correspondence with Don John in clear, and tells him in cipher that there is nothing more to expect from Madrid.

The record, text and translation →

The cipher

  • A numerical syllabary: a number for the consonant (6 d, 7 c, 15 l, 16 m, 17 n, 20 p, 22 r, 23 s, 24 t…), a mark after the number for the vowel (+ a, . e, 6 i, hook o, ı u).
  • Superscript signs for n, s, r and l; numbers alone for isolated vowels.
  • A variant of the 1577 table of the Genoa embassy: with Pérez, 8 stands for g (b in Genoa) and “8 with a small 2” for ble.

How we read it

  1. A table rebuilt from cipher / “descifrada” pairs of the Genoa despatches kept at Simancas, then adapted to Pérez (key K_P).
  2. A declared failure: a first pair validation (Estado 1410,69–70) gives 72.4% of words, below the 75% threshold set in advance; the key is not validated.
  3. A validation on a fresh pair, under an amendment to the protocol written and hashed beforehand: the corrected key K_P2, frozen, applied to twelve lines of the Genoa despatch of 19 July 1577 (Estado 1410,65, 387 characters), transcribed in two passes and frozen before opening its period decipherment (1410,66): 81.3% of words and 87.9% of characters recovered, against at best 16.5% and 47.8% for 200 control keys.
  4. The reading of Pérez’s letter, doubtful signs re-checked on the full-resolution images: 60 certain words, 9 probable, 1 unresolved.

What remains uncertain

  • A short text: 70 ciphered words, 9 of them probable; one word (‹ningun›, “no”) remains unresolved, and the exact sense of “estragar” is uncertain.
  • Prior work. Checked on 29 October and again on 14 November 2026: Mignet (1845), CODOIN, G. Muro (1877, full-text search), C. Fernández Duro, P. Ávila Seoane (2024), Daniel Bourdeau’s repository (target perez1578, our reading), Cryptiana, online search. Published in part: the clear paragraph on the death of King Sebastian (“Y aunque V. A. no ha menester ni consejos ni ejemplos…”) was printed by A. Rodríguez Villa in an appendix to B. Porreño, Historia del sereníssimo señor D. Juan de Austria (Madrid, 1899), no. LXXX, p. 516, and reprinted by G. Marañón, Antonio Pérez, vol. II, appendix XXXIX. Neither gives the four cipher passages: our reading remains, to our knowledge, the first published decipherment.
